chapters.title: Chapter 5: Behavioral Economics in Organizations and the Workplace

lessons.title: Groupthink in Boardrooms: How Committees Amplify Bias

children.text: A board unanimously approves a large acquisition. Six months later, when it's clearly failing, three directors privately admit they had serious doubts in the room that day. Nobody had lied. Nobody had been fooled. Each of them had simply looked around the table, seen everyone else nodding, assumed their own doubt must be the uninformed one, and stayed quiet. The board didn't fail because any individual director was foolish. It failed because the group, as a group, was worse than its worst-informed member would have been alone. This is groupthink, and it closes this chapter by explaining why committees can amplify exactly the biases this course has spent five chapters describing in individuals.

body.text: A cohesive group under pressure to reach consensus can suppress its own members' honest doubts so effectively that the final decision is worse than what almost any individual member privately believed was right. The failure isn't a lack of expertise in the room. It's a social dynamic that makes the expertise in the room impossible to use.

markDefs.definition: Psychologist Irving Janis's term for a mode of thinking that cohesive groups fall into when the drive for consensus and harmony overrides members' realistic appraisal of alternative courses of action.

children.text: in 1972, studying a series of major US policy fiascoes, most famously the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, where a group of genuinely capable, experienced advisors collectively approved a plan riddled with flaws that individual members later admitted they'd privately questioned at the time. Janis catalogued a set of recurring symptoms across these cases. Four matter most directly for a corporate boardroom: the illusion of unanimity, mistaking group silence for group agreement; self-censorship, individually suppressing your own doubts to avoid disrupting apparent consensus; direct pressure on dissenters, subtly or explicitly pushing anyone who raises an objection back into line; and self-appointed mindguards, someone who screens out uncomfortable information before it ever reaches the group or its leader.
Why Groupthink Isn't the Same as an Information Cascade

Chapter 3 covered information cascades, where individuals, often strangers who never speak to one another, rationally infer from others' observed choices and end up copying the crowd. Groupthink is a related but distinct failure, specific to a cohesive, actively interacting group under social pressure to maintain harmony. A cascade can happen entirely silently, through revealed choices alone. Groupthink requires people in a room together, actively, if unintentionally, suppressing dissenting information from each other, often reinforced by an insulated group culture, a lack of impartial leadership, and high-stakes time pressure that makes open debate feel like a costly delay rather than useful friction.

body.caption: Two related but distinct group failures

cells: No, works even among strangers who never speak
Yes, requires a cohesive, interacting group
Rationally inferring from others' observed choices
Social pressure to preserve group harmony and consensus
Applicants piling into a heavily oversubscribed IPO

children.text: Real-World Governance Response: SEBI's Independent Director Framework

markDefs.definition: A director with no material pecuniary relationship with the company, its promoters, or management, required in minimum proportion on listed company boards under SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, partly to provide a genuinely independent perspective.

children.text: India's corporate governance framework already builds in a structural defence against exactly this dynamic. SEBI's LODR Regulations require listed companies to maintain a minimum proportion of

on the board, generally at least one-third, rising to at least half where the chairperson isn't a non-executive, independent director themselves, alongside requirements for an independent-director-majority Audit Committee. The logic maps directly onto Janis's diagnosis: a board made up entirely of executives with career and financial stakes tied to the group's own decisions is structurally primed for self-censorship and mindguarding. A genuinely independent director, with no such stake, is far better positioned to be the person willing to voice the doubt everyone else is privately holding, provided the board's culture actually makes room for them to do so.
Janis's Own Prescriptions: Designing Against Groupthink

Janis didn't just diagnose the failure, he proposed specific structural fixes, several of which reach back to ideas already covered in this course. He recommended the group's leader withhold their own opinion until late in a discussion, directly to avoid anchoring the room the way Chapter 3 covered for negotiation and pricing. He recommended assigning a rotating devil's advocate role, so dissent becomes an assigned job rather than a personal risk. He recommended splitting into independent sub-groups to deliberate separately before reconvening, so the group doesn't converge on a shared view before anyone has genuinely tested it alone. And he recommended a formal second-chance meeting, a scheduled pause after a decision feels finalized, specifically to surface any remaining doubts before it becomes irreversible.

body.title: A board's anti-groupthink checklist
steps: Have the chair or most senior voice share their view last, not first, so it doesn't anchor the discussion
Assign a rotating devil's advocate role for major decisions, so dissent is an assigned duty rather than a personal risk
Ensure independent directors genuinely participate in, not just attend, high-stakes discussions
Split into smaller sub-groups to deliberate separately before reconvening on major decisions
Schedule a second-chance meeting before finalizing any high-stakes decision, specifically inviting lingering doubts

body.title: Diagnosing a boardroom failure
body.scenario: A startup's board approves a major pivot in strategy after a 20-minute discussion. The CEO, who proposed the pivot, is well-liked and has been right before. Two directors later admit privately they had reservations about the plan's core assumption but didn't raise them, since "everyone else seemed convinced" and they didn't want to be the one who derailed a decision the room clearly wanted to make.
body.prompt: Which groupthink symptoms from this lesson are visible here, and what specific process change would have most directly addressed them?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The two directors' silence, mistaken by the rest of the room as agreement, is the illusion of unanimity in action, and their private decision not to voice a real doubt is self-censorship, exactly as Janis described.
2. The CEO proposing the pivot and presumably speaking early and confidently risks anchoring the room, making dissent feel like contradicting a well-liked leader with a good track record rather than raising a genuine analytical concern.
3. The 20-minute discussion window is itself a risk factor, not enough time for a rotating devil's advocate, a sub-group exercise, or a genuine second look, all of which Janis specifically recommended for exactly this kind of high-stakes, time-pressured decision.
4. The most direct fix would have been structural: the CEO withholding a strong personal recommendation until after others spoke, an assigned devil's advocate for this specific decision, and explicitly asking each director in turn for their view rather than accepting general nodding as consensus.

body.title: Groupthink, or an information cascade?
body.question: A group of retail investors, none of whom know each other, each independently decide to apply for an IPO after seeing its subscription numbers climb throughout the day on a public dashboard. Which mechanism from this course is this?
options: Groupthink, because a large group is converging on the same decision
An information cascade, because the investors are inferring from others' revealed public actions without any direct social interaction or pressure to conform
Escalation of commitment, because investors don't want to admit they hesitated earlier
The endowment effect, because investors feel they already own the shares
body.explanation: No direct interaction, shared identity, or social pressure to preserve group harmony is present here, only individuals independently reading a public signal, the defining feature of an information cascade rather than groupthink, which specifically requires a cohesive, interacting group.

body.title: Name the symptom
body.textWithBlank: Mistaking a group's silence for genuine agreement, when members are actually suppressing their own private doubts, is called the illusion of ___.
body.explanation: The illusion of unanimity is one of Irving Janis's core groupthink symptoms, and it's specifically dangerous because it's invisible from inside the room: everyone sees apparent agreement and assumes their own doubt must be the outlier.

body.title: Why the Bay of Pigs, specifically?

children.text: Janis chose the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, a failed US-backed attempt to overthrow Cuba's government, as his central case study because the decision-making group involved was unusually well-qualified on paper: experienced advisors, extensive intelligence resources, and a president known for seeking out multiple viewpoints on other decisions. Several participants later acknowledged private doubts about the plan's core assumptions that were never raised in the room. Janis's point was precisely that groupthink isn't a symptom of a weak or poorly staffed group. It can happen to highly capable people, which is exactly why structural safeguards matter more than simply trusting a room full of smart people to speak up on their own.

body.label: Groupthink's origin
body.context: Irving Janis coined the term studying major policy fiascoes, finding the failure wasn't a lack of expertise in the room, but a social dynamic that made the expertise impossible to use.

cards.definition: A cohesive group's drive for consensus overriding its members' realistic appraisal of alternatives, coined by Irving Janis in 1972.
Mistaking a group's silence for genuine agreement, when members are privately self-censoring their own doubts.
A self-appointed group member who screens out uncomfortable or dissenting information before it reaches the group or its leader.
A role, ideally rotating, formally assigned to argue against the group's emerging consensus, converting dissent from a personal risk into an assigned duty.
A director with no material financial ties to a company's promoters or management, required in minimum proportion under SEBI's LODR Regulations, structurally positioned to counter groupthink.

points: Groupthink happens when a cohesive group's drive for consensus overrides its members' honest, individual judgment, producing a collective decision worse than what most members privately believed.

It is distinct from an information cascade: groupthink requires an interacting, cohesive group under social pressure, while a cascade can happen silently among strangers simply observing each other's choices.

SEBI's independent director requirements are a structural, regulatory response to exactly this failure mode, built on the same logic Janis identified: people with no personal stake in the group's prior decisions are better positioned to voice dissent.

Janis's own prescriptions, a rotating devil's advocate, the leader speaking last, independent sub-group deliberation, and a scheduled second-chance meeting, turn dissent from a personal social risk into a designed, expected part of the process.

This closes Chapter 5's throughline: retirement defaults, incentive design, sunk cost, and groupthink are all cases where the same individual-level biases from earlier chapters get amplified, or sometimes counteracted, by organizational structure. Chapter 6 zooms out one final time, to where these same forces play out across entire markets and economies.
